title: MDCAT English: Commonly Missed Question Types
excerpt: English is a small section of the MDCAT paper, but it's also one of the easiest to lose marks on unnecessarily. Here's where students commonly slip, and how to close those gaps.

content.text: A small section that's easy to underestimate

English makes up a small slice of the MDCAT paper compared to Biology, Chemistry, or Physics — which is exactly why so many students give it almost no dedicated prep time. That's a mistake. When merit lists are separated by small margins, a section you could realistically score close to full marks on, with a fraction of the study time Biology demands, isn't one to leave to chance.

Confirm the exact number of English MCQs and the current topic list against the official PMDC syllabus before finalizing how much time you budget for this section — treat the guidance below as where to focus within English, not a substitute for the syllabus itself.

The section generally draws on grammar, vocabulary, and reading comprehension at a level consistent with what you've already covered in FSc English — but MDCAT tests it through multiple-choice questions with deliberately close distractors, which rewards precision over general familiarity with the language.
Tenses: the single most tested grammar topic

Across past papers, tenses come up more consistently than any other single grammar area. Students who read English comfortably often still slip here, because tense questions in an MCQ format aren't testing whether you can construct a sentence correctly in conversation — they're testing whether you can spot the one grammatically correct option among several that all sound plausible.

The fix is targeted practice with sentence-correction and fill-in-the-blank tense questions specifically, rather than general reading. Reading fluency and MCQ-format tense accuracy are related but not the same skill.
Active/passive voice and direct/indirect speech: rules that need drilling, not just recognition

These two areas show up repeatedly alongside tenses, and they share a common trap: you can recognize a passive sentence or reported speech when you read it, but converting between forms under exam pressure is a different skill. Missing a single word — a modal verb, a pronoun shift, a tense change that's required when converting speech — is enough to flip a correct answer into a wrong one.

items: Practice full conversions (active to passive and back), not just identification
Pay close attention to the specific rules for modal verbs and tense shifts in reported speech, since these are where most errors happen

content.text: Subject-verb agreement: the "obvious" topic that isn't

Subject-verb agreement feels basic, which is precisely why it trips students up — MDCAT questions in this area often use compound subjects, collective nouns, or phrases between the subject and verb that make the correct verb form less obvious than it looks at first glance. A quick read-through can miss these; a deliberate check of what the actual subject of the sentence is usually catches them.
Vocabulary: precision over volume

Vocabulary questions — synonyms, antonyms, and analogies — reward words you've seen used in context, not just words you've memorized from a list the night before. A common mistake is cramming long word lists close to the exam without ever seeing those words in a sentence; the meaning doesn't stick, and MDCAT vocabulary questions are built around subtle distinctions between similar words, which flat memorization doesn't prepare you for.

A steadier approach — a smaller number of new words each day, encountered in context through reading, rather than a large list crammed right before the exam — tends to hold up better under exam conditions.
Reading comprehension: speed is the real bottleneck

Comprehension questions aren't usually where students get the content wrong — they're where students run out of time. Because English is a small section relative to the whole paper, it's tempting to under-practice timed reading, but comprehension passages reward the ability to scan for the specific detail a question is asking about rather than reading every line closely.

Practicing the difference between skimming for the general idea and scanning for a specific answer — and doing this under a timer, not just untimed — is what actually improves comprehension speed. Reading widely in English also helps, but it's a slower-acting fix; timed practice with MDCAT-style passages closes the gap faster.
Because there's no negative marking, never leave an English question blank — even an educated guess based on eliminating one or two obviously wrong options is better than skipping it.
A simple way to close these gaps
Given how small this section is, a modest, consistent routine tends to outperform occasional long study sessions:

items: A short daily block on tenses, voice, and speech conversion — the grammar areas most consistently tested
A handful of new vocabulary words a day, learned in context rather than as an isolated list
Regular timed reading comprehension practice, specifically to build scanning speed
A dedicated pass on subject-verb agreement, since it's easy to assume you already know it well enough

content.text: The bottom line

English won't decide your MDCAT result on its own, but losing marks here usually isn't about not knowing the language — it's about specific, well-known trouble spots: tenses, voice and speech conversion, subject-verb agreement in tricky constructions, imprecise vocabulary prep, and reading comprehension under time pressure. A small, steady amount of targeted practice on these specific areas is enough to turn this section into close to guaranteed marks, freeing up more of your attention for Biology, Chemistry, and Physics.

items.question: What grammar topic is most commonly tested in MDCAT English?
items.answer: Tenses come up more consistently than any other single grammar area across past papers. The MCQ format tests whether you can spot the one grammatically correct option among several plausible-sounding ones, which is a different skill from general conversational fluency.

items.question: How should I prepare for active/passive voice and direct/indirect speech questions?
items.answer: Practice full conversions between forms, not just recognizing them when you read them. Pay close attention to modal verbs and tense shifts required in reported speech, since these small details are where most errors happen under exam pressure.

items.question: Is memorizing vocabulary lists an effective way to prepare?
items.answer: Not as effective as learning words in context. Cramming word lists without seeing them used in sentences means the meaning doesn't stick, and MDCAT vocabulary questions test subtle distinctions between similar words that flat memorization doesn't prepare you for.

items.question: Why do students lose marks on reading comprehension if their English is strong?
items.answer: Usually it's a time problem, not a comprehension problem. The section rewards scanning for the specific detail a question asks about rather than reading every line closely — building that scanning speed requires timed practice with MDCAT-style passages, not just general reading.

items.question: Should I skip a question in the English section if I'm unsure of the answer?
items.answer: No — since MDCAT has no negative marking, an educated guess after eliminating one or two clearly wrong options is always better than leaving a question blank.
